items.stem: In December 1964, Berkeley student Mario Savio told a crowd that when "the operation of the machine becomes so odious," people must put their "bodies upon the gears" to stop it. Savio was a leader of the Free Speech Movement. What was the movement challenging?

stimulus.text: "There is a time when the operation of the machine becomes so odious, makes you so sick at heart, that you can't take part... you've got to put your bodies upon the gears and upon the wheels." — Mario Savio, speech at the University of California, Berkeley, December 1964.

options: (A) The university's ban on student political activity on campus
(B) The federal draft that sent young men to fight in the Vietnam War
(C) Racial segregation in Berkeley's public elementary and high schools
(D) The rising cost of tuition at California's public universities
items.explanation: The Free Speech Movement began as a fight over the university's rules against student political organizing on campus; Savio's "machine" was the university administration itself.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The movement started when Berkeley banned student political activity on campus, and Savio's speech attacked the university "machine."
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Opposition to the draft grew later in the decade; the 1964 fight was about campus speech rules.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The movement was about student political rights on campus, not the city's public schools.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Tuition costs were not the issue; the fight was over political activity rules.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 Youth culture and counterculture — the Free Speech Movement at Berkeley (1964), Mario Savio urging students to put their "bodies upon the gears" of the university machine

items.stem: Students for a Democratic Society (SDS) turned universities into protest headquarters in the 1960s. By the late 1960s, opposition to the Vietnam War dominated campus protest. What most directly explains why Vietnam, rather than another issue, became the center of campus protest?
options: (A) The war enjoyed widespread popularity among college students
(B) The draft made the war personal for college-age men
(C) Universities required their students to enlist after graduation
(D) Congress had banned every other form of student protest
items.explanation: The draft gave millions of students a direct personal stake in the war, which is why Vietnam and the draft became the dominant campus issues.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The war was deeply unpopular on campuses; that unpopularity drove the protests.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The draft meant the war could pull students themselves into combat, making it personal.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Universities did not require enlistment; the federal draft was the mechanism.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. No such ban existed; students protested many issues, but Vietnam dominated because of the draft.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 Youth culture and counterculture — SDS turned universities into protest headquarters over civil rights and, above all, Vietnam and the draft

items.stem: A historian claims that the Woodstock festival proves most young Americans joined the counterculture, since some 400,000 young people gathered in a muddy New York field in August 1969. Which evaluation of this claim is best supported?

stimulus.text: The Woodstock festival of August 1969 — some 400,000 young people in a muddy New York field — became the counterculture's defining image.

options: (A) The claim is fully supported: 400,000 attendees were a majority of the nation's youth
(B) Shared rock music proves that every young person in America held the same politics
(C) The claim mistakes a powerful image for the whole generation
(D) The claim fails because Woodstock drew only a sparse, small crowd
items.explanation: Woodstock's power was symbolic and media-driven; 400,000 people, while huge for a festival, were a small fraction of the baby-boom generation, most of whom did not live the counterculture life.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Four hundred thousand was a tiny fraction of the tens of millions of young Americans.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Shared music did not mean shared politics or lifestyles.
option_explanations.C: Correct. A defining image is not a census; most youth did not attend Woodstock or join communes.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Woodstock was massively attended; the problem with the claim is what attendance proves, not the turnout.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 Youth culture and counterculture — the Woodstock festival of August 1969, some 400,000 young people in a muddy New York field, became the counterculture's defining image

items.stem: The wider 1960s counterculture embraced communes, psychedelic drugs, long hair, and a "do your own thing" ethic centered in places like San Francisco's Haight-Ashbury. What was this counterculture rejecting?
options: (A) The goals and methods of the civil rights movement in the South
(B) American popular music and the radio stations that played it
(C) The idea that respectable young people should attend college
(D) The postwar package: careers, suburbs, and conformity
items.explanation: The review describes the counterculture as rejecting "the whole package" their parents had built — the career-and-suburb conformity of postwar middle-class life.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The counterculture generally sympathized with civil rights; it rejected middle-class conformity, not racial equality.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Rock music was the counterculture's common language, not its target.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Many counterculture figures were college students or dropouts; college itself was not the target.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Communes, long hair, and "do your own thing" were rejections of careers, suburbs, and conformity.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 Youth culture and counterculture — a wider counterculture rejected the whole package: communes, psychedelic drugs, long hair, and a "do your own thing" ethic centered in places like San Francisco's Haight-Ashbury

items.stem: The generation gap between baby-boom youth and their parents became a political force in the late 1960s rather than remaining a private family quarrel. What most directly explains that transformation?
options: (A) Nixon gave the backlash a name and turned it into votes
(B) Young people began voting in larger numbers than their parents
(C) The generation gap ended when the voting age was lowered to 18
(D) Hippies and their parents reached agreement on the Vietnam War
items.explanation: Nixon's 1969 appeal to the "silent majority" organized non-protesting Americans politically, converting cultural resentment into an electoral coalition.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Naming the "silent majority" gave the backlash a political identity and a place in Nixon's coalition.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Older Americans voted at high rates; the mechanism was Nixon's mobilization of their resentment, not a youth turnout surge.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The voting age was lowered in 1971, after the backlash had already become political.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Vietnam was a central source of the disagreement, not a point of agreement.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 Youth culture and counterculture — Nixon's 1969 appeal to the "silent majority" of Americans who didn't protest gave the resentment a name and a politics

items.stem: Nixon's 1969 appeal counterposed the "silent majority" of non-protesting Americans against demonstrators and the counterculture. In the review's account, what did that backlash stand for?
options: (A) Immediate withdrawal from Vietnam and amnesty for draft resisters
(B) Law and order, patriotism, and traditional values
(C) Expanded federal aid to universities
(D) Support for commune living and psychedelic drugs
items.explanation: The review defines the backlash's politics as law and order, patriotism, and traditional values set against longhairs and demonstrators.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. That was the antiwar movement's position, the opposite of the backlash.
option_explanations.B: Correct. These were the values Nixon's appeal mobilized against protesters and the counterculture.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The backlash treated campuses as battlegrounds, not as places deserving more federal aid.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The backlash opposed the counterculture's lifestyle; it did not support it.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 Youth culture and counterculture — Nixon's 1969 appeal to the "silent majority"; the politics was law and order, patriotism, and traditional values against longhairs and demonstrators

items.stem: Rock music became the 1960s generation's common language. What does that fact show about American youth in the decade?
options: (A) They shared a culture that crossed regions and campuses
(B) They all agreed with one another about politics
(C) Older Americans embraced rock music as their own music
(D) The music industry actively opposed the counterculture's values
items.explanation: A common musical language meant youth in different places shared cultural reference points, forming a generation-wide youth culture.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Shared music created shared culture across the country's campuses and cities.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Shared tastes did not mean shared politics; the generation was politically divided.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The generation gap meant older Americans largely rejected the music.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The industry sold the music widely; it did not oppose the culture it profited from.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 Youth culture and counterculture — rock music became the generation's common language

items.stem: The Free Speech Movement of 1964 fought campus speech rules at Berkeley; later in the decade, student protest targeted the Vietnam War. What is the best historical connection between the two?
options: (A) The Free Speech Movement directly caused the Vietnam War to begin
(B) Antiwar protesters abandoned campus organizing entirely after 1965
(C) Campus protest networks built in 1964 carried into the antiwar movement
(D) The Free Speech Movement had opposed the Vietnam War from its beginning in 1964
items.explanation: The review presents campuses as protest headquarters across the decade; the organizing capacity built in 1964 was available when Vietnam and the draft became the dominant issues.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The war's causes lay in foreign policy, not in a Berkeley protest.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Campuses remained the headquarters of protest throughout the decade.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The continuity is organizational: 1964 built the campus protest infrastructure the antiwar movement then used.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. In 1964 the fight was about campus speech rules; Vietnam became central later as the war and the draft escalated.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 Youth culture and counterculture — the Free Speech Movement at Berkeley (1964) and SDS turned universities into protest headquarters over civil rights and, above all, Vietnam and the draft

items.stem: The review argues that the counterculture hardened the conservative coalition that would elect Reagan. How did the counterculture produce that result?
options: (A) By provoking a backlash hardened around law and order and traditional values
(B) By splitting the national Democratic Party over the issue of civil rights legislation
(C) By persuading most ordinary Americans to adopt hippie lifestyles
(D) By ending the Vietnam War through sustained campus protest
items.explanation: The counterculture's visibility provoked the "silent majority" backlash, which became a durable conservative coalition organized around traditional values.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Backlash against the counterculture gave conservatives a unifying cause and a coalition.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The mechanism in the review is the cultural backlash, not the civil-rights split in the Democratic Party.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Most Americans did not become hippies; they reacted against the counterculture.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The war ended for other reasons; the coalition-building mechanism was the backlash.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 Youth culture and counterculture — the counterculture hardened the conservative coalition that would elect Reagan

items.stem: San Francisco's Haight-Ashbury became a famous center of the 1960s counterculture. What did such places provide?
options: (A) Military recruiting stations supporting the Vietnam War effort
(B) A community living out the "do your own thing" ethic in communes
(C) The headquarters for Nixon's 1968 presidential campaign
(D) New suburban housing developments built for young families
items.explanation: Haight-Ashbury was where the counterculture's ethic was lived out collectively — communes, shared households, and street life — not just discussed.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The counterculture opposed the war and the draft; it did not staff recruiting stations.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The neighborhood was the counterculture's most famous lived community.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Nixon's campaign had no connection to Haight-Ashbury.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Haight-Ashbury was an urban neighborhood, the opposite of a suburb.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 Youth culture and counterculture — a "do your own thing" ethic centered in places like San Francisco's Haight-Ashbury
